docs.title: Trustfall language reference
docs.text:
Trustfall's data model is a graph...

Before we can query a dataset with Trustfall, we have to write a schema. For a guide on writing a schema there's the Trustfall schema guide.

Once you have a schema you can start writing queries. For a guide on writing a query there's the Trustfall query reference.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Let's define the meaning of common pieces of Trustfall terminology.

This page references a hypothetical social media app ("Flutter") as an example with which to explain Trustfall concepts. In Flutter, users may post public messages, "like" each other's posts, and follow other users' activity.

docs.title: schema
docs.text:
A formal description of the shape of a data set.

The schema is used to validate and type-check queries, making sure they are valid before attempting to execute them. It also powers IDE conveniences such as code auto-complete.

It describes different types of vertices, each of which contains properties and may be connected to other vertices via named edges.

docs.title: vertex
docs.text:
A single data item in a Trustfall dataset. In our Flutter example app, each user's profile would be represented as a separate vertex.

Its shape is described by its vertex type: it contains a set of properties, and may be connected to other vertices via edges.

The equivalent concept in SQL is a row in a table.

docs.title: vertex type
docs.text:
A shape of vertex data items, as described in the schema.

In our Flutter example app, User and Post are two of the vertex types. The User type is defined like this:

type User {
    # properties
    username: String!]]]
    display_name: String
    # ...

    # edges
    posts: [Post!]
    follows: [User!]
    # ...
}

The equivalent concept in SQL is a table.

docs.title: property
docs.text:
A named and typed value that each vertex of a given vertex type contains.

In our Flutter example app, the User vertex type has properties like username of type String! (non-nullable string).

The equivalent concept in SQL is a column.

docs.title: edge
docs.text:
A named relationship that one vertex type might have to another vertex type, or an instance of such a relationship between two specific vertices.

In our Flutter example app, the User vertex type has a posts edge that represents the messages that a user has posted. Each User vertex may be connected to zero, one, or more Post vertices via instances of the posts edge.

The equivalent concept in SQL is a foreign key relationship.

docs.title: entrypoint
docs.text:
A starting point for Trustfall queries in a given schema.

In our Flutter example app, entrypoints include: - Looking up a User vertex by their username. - Listing messages that are currently popular.

SQL doesn't have an equivalent concept since querying may begin at any table. Trustfall supports querying any data source, not just SQL, and many data sources do not allow listing all instances of a particular data point. For example, GitHub doesn't support enumerating all its millions of registered users, so the equivalent of a SQL SELECT * FROM GitHubUser query is not possible against the GitHub APIs. In Trustfall, we model these querying restrictions by separating the vertex types from the entrypoints where querying may begin.

docs.title: query
docs.text: A Trustfall query is a request for data, written in a GraphQL-like syntax, that specifies which data to retrieve and how to filter, transform, and aggregate it. Queries start from an entrypoint, traverse edges between vertices, and use directives to control the output.

docs.title: adapter
docs.text: A Trustfall plugin that enables querying a specific dataset with the Trustfall query interpreter. It acts as a connector between the Trustfall APIs and the underlying data source, which might be a file format, an API, a database, etc.

docs.title: directive
docs.text: A component of a query that describes an operation to be performed, such as filtering or transforming the data. Directives are prefixed with the @ symbol: @filter, @output, etc.

docs.title: Trustfall query reference
docs.text: Trustfall queries are written in a GraphQL-like syntax and support powerful querying capabilities including filtering, aggregation, recursion, and optional traversals.

docs.title: Query structure
docs.text:
Every Trustfall query starts from an entrypoint defined in the schema and traverses through vertices and edges to select and filter data.

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
Trustfall queries may make use of several directives:

  • @output - Mark fields to include in query results
  • @filter - Filter vertices based on property values
  • @tag - Save values for use in later filters
  • @optional - Make edges optional (like SQL LEFT JOIN)
  • @recurse - Follow edges recursively to arbitrary depth
  • @fold - Aggregate multiple results into lists
  • @transform - Transform values (e.g., counting)

docs.title: Type coercions
docs.text:
Type coercions allow narrowing vertices to more specific types:

  • Type coercions - Filter and process vertices by their specific type

docs.title: Edge parameters
docs.text:
Edges can accept parameters to control traversal:

  • Edge parameters - Pass arguments when traversing edges

docs.title: Comprehensive examples
docs.text:
For complete examples demonstrating all features:

  • Query examples - Comprehensive examples of all query features

docs.title: Basic query
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        email @output
    }
}

docs.title: With filtering
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        age @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_age"])
    }
}

docs.title: With aggregation
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: With optional edges
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional {
            latest_title: title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: With recursion
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        follows @recurse(depth: 3) {
            friend: username @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: With type coercion
docs.text:
{
    Number(max: 10) {
        value @output
        ... on Prime {
            is_prime: value @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Edge Parameters
docs.text: Edge parameters allow you to pass arguments when traversing an edge, enabling filtered or parameterized traversals defined by the schema.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Edges can accept parameters as defined in the schema:

{
    Directory {
        name @output

        # Traverse to files with .txt extension
        files(extension: "txt") {
            name @output
        }
    }
}

This traverses only to files matching the specified extension.

docs.title: Required vs optional parameters
docs.text:
The schema defines which parameters are required and which are optional:

{
    User {
        username @output

        # Parameter is required
        posts(limit: 10) {
            title @output
        }

        # Parameter is optional (has default value)
        follows(active_only: true) {
            username @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Using variables in parameters
docs.text:
Edge parameters commonly use query variables:

{
    Repository {
        name @output

        issues(state: "$issue_state") {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

With variables: {"issue_state": "open"}

docs.title: Multiple parameters
docs.text:
Edges can accept multiple parameters:

{
    Post {
        title @output

        comments(min_likes: "$min", max_likes: "$max") {
            text @output
            likes @output
        }
    }
}

With variables: {"min": 5, "max": 100}

docs.title: Parameter types
docs.text: Parameters can have different types as defined in the schema:

docs.title: String parameters
docs.text:
{
    Directory {
        files(extension: "pdf") {
            name @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Integer parameters
docs.text:
{
    User {
        posts(limit: 20) {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Boolean parameters
docs.text:
{
    Repository {
        issues(include_closed: false) {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: List parameters
docs.text:
{
    Post {
        comments(categories: ["tech", "science"]) {
            text @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Nullable parameters
docs.text:
Parameters can be nullable, allowing null as a valid value:

{
    User {
        # null means "no filter on creation date"
        posts(created_after: null) {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Default parameter values
docs.text:
If the schema defines a default value, you can omit the parameter:

{
    User {
        # Uses default limit defined in schema
        posts {
            title @output
        }

        # Overrides default
        recent_posts: posts(limit: 5) {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Parameters vs filters
docs.text: Edge parameters and @filter directives serve different purposes:

docs.title: Edge parameters
docs.text:
• Defined by the schema for specific edges
  • May affect which edges exist or are traversed
  • Applied at the edge traversal level

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
• Generic filtering mechanism
  • Applied to vertex properties
  • Work on vertices reached through edges
{
    Directory {
        # Edge parameter: limits traversal to .txt files
        files(extension: "txt") {
            # Filter: further filters to files larger than min_size
            size @filter(op: ">", value: ["$min_size"])
                 @output
            name @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Parameters with optional edges
docs.text:
Parameters work with @optional edges:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts(category: "tech") @optional {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Users without tech posts are included with null for title.

docs.title: Parameters with fold
docs.text:
Parameters filter which items are included in the fold:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts(min_likes: 10) @fold {
            popular_post: title @output
        }
    }
}

Only posts with at least 10 likes are included in the folded list.

docs.title: Parameters with recurse
docs.text:
Parameterized edges can be used with recursion:

{
    Directory {
        name @output

        subdirectory(max_depth: 3) @recurse(depth: 5) {
            name @output
        }
    }
}

The parameter applies at each level of recursion.

docs.title: Semantic differences with optional and recurse
docs.text: When using edge parameters with @optional or @recurse, the parameters become part of the edge's existence condition:

docs.title: With @optional
docs.text:
# Edge parameter approach
{
    Directory {
        files(extension: "txt") @optional {
            name @output
        }
    }
}

This is different from:

# Filter approach
{
    Directory {
        files @optional {
            extension @filter(op: "=", value: ["$ext"])
            name @output
        }
    }
}

In the first case (parameter), if no .txt files exist, the result is null. In the second case (filter), if files exist but none are .txt, the result is still null, but the edge is considered to exist.

docs.title: With @recurse
docs.text:
# Edge parameter approach
{
    User {
        follows(active: true) @recurse(depth: 3) {
            username @output
        }
    }
}

Only follows active users at each level of recursion. An inactive user stops that path of recursion.

# Filter approach
{
    User {
        follows @recurse(depth: 3) {
            active @filter(op: "=", value: ["$active"])
            username @output
        }
    }
}

Follows all users but only outputs those who are active. Recursion continues through inactive users.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output

        posts(offset: "$offset", limit: "$limit") {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

With variables: {"offset": 0, "limit": 20}

docs.title: Date range filtering
docs.text:
{
    Repository {
        name @output

        commits(since: "$start_date", until: "$end_date") {
            message @output
            timestamp @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Category filtering
docs.text:
{
    Blog {
        title @output

        posts(category: "$category") @fold {
            post_title: title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Combined with count
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output

        posts(status: "published") 
              @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @output(name: "published_count")
    }
}

docs.title: Schema definition required
docs.text:
Edge parameters must be defined in the schema. You cannot add arbitrary parameters to edges:

# Invalid if 'foo' parameter is not defined in schema
{
    User {
        posts(foo: "bar") {  # Error!
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Type safety
docs.text:
Parameter values must match the type defined in the schema:

# Invalid: passing string when integer expected
{
    User {
        posts(limit: "10") {  # Error! Should be 10 not "10"
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Required parameters must be provided
docs.text:
If a parameter is required (non-nullable without a default), it must be provided:

# Invalid if 'category' is required
{
    Post {
        comments {  # Error! Missing required parameter
            text @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Query Examples
docs.text: This page provides comprehensive examples of Trustfall queries demonstrating all features of the query language.

docs.title: Simple property selection
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        email @output
    }
}

Returns all users with their username and email.

docs.title: Using entrypoint parameters
docs.text:
{
    FindUser(username: "alice") {
        username @output
        display_name @output
    }
}

Finds a specific user by username.

docs.title: Basic equality filter
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        age @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_age"]) @output
    }
}

With variables: {"min_age": 18}

docs.title: String filters
docs.text:
{
    Post {
        title @filter(op: "has_prefix", value: ["$prefix"])
              @output
        content @filter(op: "has_substring", value: ["$keyword"])
                @output
    }
}

With variables: {"prefix": "Introduction", "keyword": "Trustfall"}

docs.title: Regex filter
docs.text:
{
    User {
        email @filter(op: "regex", value: ["$email_pattern"])
              @output
    }
}

With variables: {"email_pattern": ".*@example\\.com$"}

docs.title: Multiple filters (AND logic)
docs.text:
{
    Post {
        likes @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_likes"])
              @filter(op: "<=", value: ["$max_likes"])
              @output
        title @output
    }
}

docs.title: Null checking
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        bio @filter(op: "is_not_null") @output
    }
}

Returns only users who have set a bio.

docs.title: List membership
docs.text:
{
    Post {
        category @filter(op: "one_of", value: ["$categories"])
                 @output
        title @output
    }
}

With variables: {"categories": ["tech", "science", "programming"]}

docs.title: Basic edge traversal
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Returns each user with each of their posts (multiple rows per user).

docs.title: Multiple edge traversals
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts {
            title @output
            comments {
                text @output
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Comparing two fields
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "uname")
               @output
        display_name @filter(op: "=", value: ["%uname"])
                     @output
    }
}

Finds users whose display name equals their username.

docs.title: Using tags across edges
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "author")
               @output
        posts {
            title @output
            author {
                username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%author"])
            }
        }
    }
}

Verifies that posts belong to the correct author.

docs.title: Multiple tags
docs.text:
{
    Post {
        title @tag(name: "post_title") @output
        author {
            username @tag(name: "author_name")
                     @output
            display_name @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%author_name"])
                         @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%post_title"])
                         @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Basic fold
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Returns one row per user with all post titles in a list.

docs.title: Counting with fold and transform
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "post_count")
    }
}

docs.title: Filtering on counts
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_posts"])
              @output(name: "post_count")
    }
}

With variables: {"min_posts": 5}

Returns only users with at least 5 posts.

docs.title: Multiple folds
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @fold {
            post_title: title @output
        }

        follows @fold {
            followed: username @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Nested folds
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output
            comments @fold {
                text @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Creates a 2D list structure.

docs.title: Fold with filtering
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @filter(op: "has_prefix", value: ["$prefix"])
                  @output
        }
    }
}

Folds only posts matching the filter.

docs.title: Basic optional
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional {
            latest_post: title @output
        }
    }
}

Returns users even if they have no posts (with null for latest_post).

docs.title: Optional with fold
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Users without posts get an empty list instead of null.

docs.title: Nested optional
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional {
            title @output
            featured_comment @optional {
                text @output
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Optional with tags
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional {
            title @tag(name: "post_title")
        }
        display_name @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%post_title"])
                     @output
    }
}

If the user has no posts, the filter is automatically satisfied.

docs.title: Basic recursion
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        follows @recurse(depth: 3) {
            friend: username @output
        }
    }
}

Follows the "follows" relationship up to 3 levels deep.

docs.title: Recursion with filters
docs.text:
{
    Directory {
        name @output
        subdirectory @recurse(depth: 10) {
            name @filter(op: "has_prefix", value: ["$prefix"])
                 @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Recursion with tags
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "origin")
               @output
        follows @recurse(depth: 5) {
            username @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%origin"])
                     @output
        }
    }
}

Finds friends of friends, excluding the original user.

docs.title: Basic type coercion
docs.text:
{
    Number(max: 20) {
        value @output
        ... on Prime {
            is_prime: value @output
        }
    }
}

Outputs is_prime only for prime numbers.

docs.title: Multiple type coercions
docs.text:
{
    SearchResults(query: "example") {
        ... on User {
            type: __typename @output
            username @output
        }
        ... on Post {
            type: __typename @output
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Type coercion with fold
docs.text:
{
    Repository {
        name @output
        issues @fold {
            ... on Bug {
                bug_title: title @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Folds only bugs, not other issue types.

docs.title: Type coercion with recursion
docs.text:
{
    Number(max: 5) {
        value @output
        successor @recurse(depth: 10) {
            ... on Prime {
                prime: value @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Follows successors but only outputs primes.

docs.title: Complex filtering and aggregation
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "author")
               @output

        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_posts"])
              @output(name: "post_count")
        {
            title @filter(op: "has_substring", value: ["$keyword"])
            author {
                username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%author"])
            }
        }
    }
}

Finds users with at least $min_posts posts containing a keyword.

docs.title: Nested queries with multiple features
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "original_user")
               @output

        follows @recurse(depth: 2) {
            username @output

            posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "post_count")

            follows @optional @fold {
                mutual: username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%original_user"])
                                 @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Complex social network analysis: finds friends of friends and identifies mutual connections.

docs.title: Advanced aggregation with type coercion
docs.text:
{
    Repository {
        name @output

        issues @fold {
            ... on Bug {
                priority @filter(op: "one_of", value: ["$high_priority"])
                         @output
            }
        }

        bugs: issues @fold 
                     @transform(op: "count")
                     @output(name: "bug_count")
        {
            ... on Bug {
                severity @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_severity"])
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Implicit names from properties
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        email @output
    }
}

Output fields: username, email

docs.title: Explicit output names
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output(name: "user_id")
        email @output(name: "user_email")
    }
}

Output fields: user_id, user_email

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
{
    User {
        user_id: username @output
        user_email: email @output
    }
}

Output fields: user_id, user_email

docs.title: Scope prefixes
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output

        authored_: posts {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Output fields: username, authored_title

docs.title: Nested scope prefixes
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output

        authored_: posts {
            post_: author {
                name @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Output fields: username, authored_post_name

docs.title: Social media query
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "current_user")
               @output
        followers @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "follower_count")

        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_posts"])
              @output(name: "post_count")
        {
            created_at @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$since_date"])
            likes @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_likes"])

            author {
                username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%current_user"])
            }
        }
    }
}

Finds active users with recent popular posts.

docs.title: Repository analysis
docs.text:
{
    Repository {
        name @output
        stars @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_stars"]) @output

        contributors @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "contributor_count")

        issues @fold {
            ... on Bug {
                status @filter(op: "=", value: ["$status"])
                severity @output
            }
        }

        pull_requests @fold 
                      @transform(op: "count")
                      @filter(op: ">", value: ["$zero"])
                      @output(name: "pr_count")
        {
            merged @filter(op: "=", value: ["$merged_status"])
        }
    }
}

Analyzes repository health metrics.

docs.title: Hierarchical data traversal
docs.text:
{
    Directory(path: "/home") {
        name @output

        subdirectory @recurse(depth: 5) {
            name @output
            size @output

            files @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "file_count")

            subdirectory @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "subdir_count")
        }
    }
}

Explores directory structure up to 5 levels deep.

docs.title: @filter directive
docs.text:
The filter directive is a way to filter on properties in your Trustfall queries. This means you can narrow down the vertices you iterate over based on various conditions. Filters can have arguments, but the simplest ones are have no arguments. An example of this would be:

name @filter(op: "is_not_null")

Here we would only select vertices where the name property isn't null. Naturally, there's a limited number of useful filters where the only input is the property in question. For the other operations where the property is compared against some input you need to either provide a query variable or a tagged value. Currently, literal values like 3 or "hi" are not valid arguments into a filter directive — they have to be passed in via variables instead.

Filters don't have logical operators. Instead, applying multiple @filter directives to a property will implicitly apply all their conditions together, as if joined with AND. Below is a toy example using the null checking filters, which is guaranteed to yield zero entries.

name @filter(op: "is_not_null") @filter(op: "is_null")

docs.title: Use with query variables
docs.text:
A query variable is a value passed in from outside the query that is prefixed with $. Below is an example of filtering for equality on a name using a variable name provided at execution time:

name @filter(op: "=", value: ["$name"])

For a list of vertex types, this filter would mean only vertices with the name equal to the supplied name would be yielded.

We can imagine this as equivalent to the following Rust code:

vertices.iter()
    .filter(|x| x.name == name);

docs.title: Use with tagged values
docs.text:
Tagged values allow us to filter using values found within the query itself.

Using the schema in the Trustfall schema guide, if we want to find users whose username is equal to their display name, we can write:

username @tag
display_name @filter(op: "=", value: ["%username"])

docs.title: If the @tag comes from an @optional scope
docs.text: An @optional directive can be applied to an edge and then values inside that edge be tagged for use in filters. Filters using these tags are only evaluated if the edge existed, if the edge wasn't present the filter expression is true.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Filtering is restricted to allowed operations and these are as follows:

  • Equality operators: = and !=
  • Comparison operators: <, <=, > and >=
  • Null-check operators: is_null and is_not_null
  • Group membership operators: one_of, not_one_of, contains and not_contains
  • String operators (each one has a not_ version as well): has_prefix, has_suffix, has_substring and regex

The following subsections contain more details about these operations.

docs.title: Equality operators
docs.text:
• = and !=

These are fairly standard equals and not-equals operators you'll be familiar with from other languages.

docs.title: Comparison operators
docs.text:
• <, <=, >, and >=

The comparison operators should be familiar from other languages, like in SQL comparison to null is false.

docs.title: Null-check operators: is_null and is_not_null
docs.text: These operators take no arguments and should only be applied to nullable properties.

docs.title: Group membership operators
docs.text:
• one_of and not_one_of
  • contains and not_contains

The one_of and not_one_of operators require the value provided to the filter is a non-nullable list of values. Constrastingly, the contains and not_contains operators require that the property is a list so the elements of the list can be checked for equality against the argument.

docs.title: String operators
docs.text:
• has_prefix, not_has_prefix, has_suffix, and not_has_suffix
  • has_substring and not_has_substring
  • regex and not_regex

The string operators require that the provided value is non-null.

docs.title: @fold directive
docs.text: The @fold directive aggregates multiple related items into lists. It's applied to edges to collect all vertices reached through that edge into a single result row, rather than creating separate rows for each vertex.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Without @fold, traversing an edge creates one result row per vertex:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

For a user with 3 posts, this produces 3 rows: 

{"username": "alice", "title": "Post 1"}
{"username": "alice", "title": "Post 2"}
{"username": "alice", "title": "Post 3"}

With @fold, all posts are aggregated into a single row:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "title": ["Post 1", "Post 2", "Post 3"]
}

docs.title: Empty folds
docs.text:
If no vertices are reached through a folded edge, the result is an empty list:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

For a user with no posts: 

{
    "username": "bob",
    "title": []
}

docs.title: Multiple outputs in a fold
docs.text:
You can output multiple properties within a fold:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output
            created_at @output
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "title": ["Post 1", "Post 2"],
    "created_at": ["2024-01-01", "2024-01-15"]
}

The lists are parallel: title[0] and created_at[0] come from the same post.

docs.title: Filtering within folds
docs.text:
Filters within a fold limit which vertices are included in the aggregation:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @filter(op: "has_prefix", value: ["$prefix"])
                  @output
        }
    }
}

With variables {"prefix": "Hello"}, only posts with titles starting with "Hello" are included in the list.

docs.title: Fold with transform
docs.text:
The @transform directive can be used with @fold to compute aggregations:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "post_count")
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "post_count": 3
}

Currently, count is the only supported transform operation. See the @transform directive documentation for details.

docs.title: Filtering on transformed folds
docs.text:
You can filter based on the count of folded items:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_posts"])
              @output(name: "post_count")
    }
}

This only returns users with at least $min_posts posts.

docs.title: Nested folds
docs.text:
Folds can be nested to create multi-dimensional lists:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold {
            title @output

            comments @fold {
                text @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "title": ["Post 1", "Post 2"],
    "text": [
        ["Comment on Post 1", "Another comment on Post 1"],
        ["Comment on Post 2"]
    ]
}

The outer list corresponds to posts, and each inner list corresponds to comments on that post.

docs.title: Using tags from outside a fold
docs.text:
Tags defined outside a fold can be used within the fold:

{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "author")
               @output

        posts @fold {
            title @output
            author {
                username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%author"])
            }
        }
    }
}

This verifies that each post's author matches the original user.

docs.title: Using tags from within a fold
docs.text:
Tags defined within a fold can only be used within that same fold, not outside it:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @fold {
            title @tag(name: "post_title")
                  @output
            # Can use %post_title here
            subtitle @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%post_title"])
        }

        # Cannot use %post_title here - it's only available within the fold
    }
}

docs.title: Fold with optional
docs.text:
Combining @fold with @optional gives you an empty list when the edge doesn't exist:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

For users without posts, title is [] (empty list) rather than null.

docs.title: Cannot fold and recurse
docs.text:
The @fold and @recurse directives cannot be used on the same edge:

# Invalid: cannot combine @fold and @recurse
{
    User {
        follows @fold @recurse(depth: 3) {
            username @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Performance implications
docs.text: Folding aggregates all reachable vertices into memory. For edges with many connections, this can consume significant memory. Use filters within folds to limit the aggregated data when possible.

docs.title: Count items without outputting them
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: ">", value: ["$threshold"]) {
            # No @output directives needed when only counting
            __typename
        }
    }
}

This filters users who have more than $threshold posts, without outputting the posts themselves.

docs.title: Fold multiple edges
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @fold {
            post_title: title @output
        }

        follows @fold {
            followed: username @output
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "post_title": ["Post 1", "Post 2"],
    "followed": ["bob", "charlie"]
}

docs.title: @optional directive
docs.text: The @optional directive is applied to edges to make them optional. It works similar to a SQL LEFT JOIN: if the edge doesn't exist, the query continues anyway, with null values for any outputs from that scope.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Without @optional, if an edge doesn't exist, the entire result is filtered out:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

This only returns users who have at least one post.

With @optional, users without posts are also included:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @optional {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Result when user has posts: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "title": "My First Post"
}

Result when user has no posts: 

{
    "username": "bob",
    "title": null
}

docs.title: Multiple optional edges
docs.text:
You can have multiple @optional edges in the same query:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional {
            post_title: title @output
        }

        follows @optional {
            followed_user: username @output
        }
    }
}

Each optional edge is evaluated independently. A user with no posts but some followers would return: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "post_title": null,
    "followed_user": "bob"
}

docs.title: Nested optional edges
docs.text:
Optional edges can be nested:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional {
            title @output

            author @optional {
                display_name @output
            }
        }
    }
}

If a user has no posts, both title and display_name are null. If a user has posts but the author data is missing, only display_name is null.

docs.title: Optional edges with filters
docs.text:
When you apply a @filter inside an @optional scope, the filter only applies if the edge exists:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional {
            title @filter(op: "has_prefix", value: ["$prefix"])
                  @output
        }
    }
}

With variables {"prefix": "Hello"}: - Users with posts starting with "Hello" return those posts - Users with posts not starting with "Hello" return null for title - Users with no posts also return null for title

docs.title: What if the edge exists but the other vertex doesn't match its @filter
docs.text:
The @optional directive will not pretend that it "didn't see" the edge. As soon as the edge is determined to exist for the given vertex, the remainder of the query proceeds as if no @optional was present.

In other words, if a user has posts, but none of them match the filter, the user will appear with title: null. The @optional only affects whether the edge exists, not whether vertices reached through that edge match their filters.

docs.title: Optional edges and tags
docs.text:
Tags defined within an @optional scope have special behavior in filters. If the optional edge doesn't exist, any filter using that tag is automatically satisfied:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional {
            title @tag(name: "post_title")
        }

        display_name @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%post_title"])
                     @output
    }
}

For users without posts: - The @optional scope produces no results - The @filter on display_name is automatically satisfied (treated as true) - The user is included in the results

For users with posts: - The filter is evaluated normally - Only users whose display name differs from their post title are included

See the @tag directive documentation for more details.

docs.title: Using optional with fold
docs.text:
You can use @optional with @fold to aggregate optional data:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

For users without posts, the title output is an empty list [] rather than null.

See the @fold directive documentation for more details on aggregation.

docs.title: @output directive
docs.text: The @output directive marks a property or field to be included in the query results. Every query must have at least one @output directive to return data.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
The simplest form of @output marks a property to be returned with its default name:

{
    User {
        username @output
    }
}

This query returns a result set where each row has a username field.

docs.title: Implicit output name
docs.text:
When you use @output without any arguments, the output field name is determined implicitly from the property name or any alias you've given it:

{
    User {
        username @output
        display_name @output
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "display_name": "Alice Smith"
}

docs.title: Explicit output names
docs.text:
You can specify a custom output name using the name parameter:

{
    User {
        username @output(name: "user_id")
        display_name @output(name: "name")
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "user_id": "alice",
    "name": "Alice Smith"
}

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
GraphQL-style aliases can be used to rename fields before applying @output:

{
    User {
        user_id: username @output
        name: display_name @output
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "user_id": "alice",
    "name": "Alice Smith"
}

docs.title: Assigning aliases to a scope
docs.text:
You can assign an alias to an entire scope (edge traversal), which acts as a prefix for all outputs within that scope:

{
    User {
        username @output

        authored_: posts {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "authored_title": "My First Post"
}

docs.title: Nesting aliased scopes
docs.text:
Aliased scopes can be nested, and their prefixes accumulate:

{
    User {
        username @output

        authored_: posts {
            post_: author {
                username @output
            }
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "authored_post_username": "alice"
}

docs.title: Implicit vs explicit output names
docs.text:
There are three ways to name an output:

  1. Implicit from property: value @output - uses the property name value
  2. Implicit from alias: alias: value @output - uses the alias name alias (plus any scope prefixes)
  3. Explicit: value @output(name: "my_output") - uses exactly my_output, ignoring aliases and prefixes
{
    User {
        # Implicit from property
        username @output

        # Implicit from alias
        user_name: username @output

        # Explicit name (ignores any prefixes or aliases)
        username @output(name: "login")
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "user_name": "alice",
    "login": "alice"
}

docs.title: Outputting from folded edges
docs.text:
When using @output inside a @fold directive, the result is a list of values:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @fold {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "title": ["My First Post", "My Second Post", "Another Post"]
}

See the @fold directive documentation for more details on aggregating data.

docs.title: @recurse directive
docs.text: The @recurse directive allows you to traverse an edge multiple times, following the same relationship repeatedly. This is useful for hierarchical or graph-structured data like file systems, organizational charts, or social networks.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
The @recurse directive is applied to an edge and requires a depth parameter:

{
    User {
        username @output

        follows @recurse(depth: 3) {
            followed_username: username @output
        }
    }
}

This query finds: - Users directly followed by the starting user (depth 1) - Users followed by those users (depth 2) - Users followed by those users (depth 3)

docs.title: Depth parameter
docs.text:
The depth parameter specifies how many times to follow the edge:

  • depth: 1 - Direct connections only (same as no recursion)
  • depth: 2 - Direct connections and their connections
  • depth: N - Up to N levels of connections
{
    Number(max: 3) {
        value @output
        successor @recurse(depth: 3) {
            next: value @output
        }
    }
}

Starting from number 3: - Depth 0: 3 - Depth 1: 4 - Depth 2: 5 - Depth 3: 6

Each starting vertex produces multiple result rows, one for each reachable vertex at each depth.

docs.title: Recursion with filters
docs.text:
You can apply filters within a recursive scope:

{
    User {
        username @output

        follows @recurse(depth: 5) {
            username @filter(op: "has_prefix", value: ["$prefix"])
                     @output
        }
    }
}

The filter applies at every level of recursion. Only users matching the filter are followed further.

docs.title: Recursion on the same type
docs.text:
Recursion often follows edges that loop back to the same type:

{
    Directory {
        name @output

        subdirectory @recurse(depth: 10) {
            subdir_name: name @output
        }
    }
}

This traverses a directory tree up to 10 levels deep.

docs.title: Recurse with tag
docs.text:
Tags can be used within recursive scopes:

{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "original")
               @output

        follows @recurse(depth: 3) {
            username @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%original"])
                     @output
        }
    }
}

This finds all users within 3 degrees of connection who have a different username than the starting user.

docs.title: Recurse with optional
docs.text:
You can make a recursive edge optional:

{
    Number(max: 5) {
        value @output

        predecessor @optional @recurse(depth: 3) {
            prev: value @output
        }
    }
}

For numbers without predecessors (like 0), the recursion stops and returns null.

docs.title: Recurse with output at multiple levels
docs.text:
Each level of recursion can produce outputs:

{
    User {
        username @output

        follows @recurse(depth: 2) {
            # This outputs at each level of recursion
            friend: username @output

            posts {
                title @output
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Recursion and type coercion
docs.text:
You can use type coercion within recursive scopes:

{
    Number(max: 10) {
        value @output

        successor @recurse(depth: 5) {
            ... on Prime {
                prime_value: value @output
            }
        }
    }
}

This follows the successor chain but only outputs values that are prime numbers.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Recursion can generate many results. A starting set of N vertices with average branching factor B and depth D can produce up to N × B^D result rows. Use filters and reasonable depth values to limit results.

docs.title: No cycles with fold
docs.text:
The @recurse and @fold directives cannot be used on the same edge:

# Invalid: cannot use both @recurse and @fold
{
    User {
        follows @recurse(depth: 3) @fold {
            username @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Schema restrictions
docs.text: Not all edges support recursion. The schema must explicitly mark an edge as recursive-capable. Attempting to use @recurse on a non-recursive edge will result in an error.

docs.title: @tag directive
docs.text: The @tag directive allows you to save a value from one part of the query and use it later in a @filter directive. This enables comparisons between different fields within the same query.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Tags are created by applying @tag to a property, and then referenced in @filter directives using the % prefix:

{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "user")
        display_name @filter(op: "=", value: ["%user"])
        username @output
    }
}

This query finds users whose display_name exactly matches their username.

docs.title: Implicit tag names
docs.text:
If you don't specify a name, the tag uses the property name or alias:

{
    User {
        username @tag
        display_name @filter(op: "=", value: ["%username"])
        username @output
    }
}

This is equivalent to the previous example with explicit tag name.

docs.title: Using tags with aliases
docs.text:
When using an alias, the tag name is derived from the alias, not the property:

{
    User {
        user: username @tag
        display_name @filter(op: "=", value: ["%user"])
        username @output
    }
}

docs.title: Tags across edges
docs.text:
Tags can be used across edge traversals to compare values at different levels:

{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "author_name")

        posts {
            title @output
            author {
                username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%author_name"])
            }
        }
    }
}

This query gets posts where the post's author matches the original user (a self-referential check).

docs.title: Tags in optional scopes
docs.text:
Tags defined within an @optional scope have special behavior. When the optional edge doesn't exist, filters using that tag are automatically considered to pass:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional {
            title @tag(name: "post_title")
        }

        display_name @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%post_title"])
    }
}

If the user has no posts, the filter on display_name is treated as true, and the user is included in results.

See the @optional directive documentation for more details.

docs.title: Multiple tags
docs.text:
You can tag multiple values and use them together:

{
    User {
        username @tag(name: "uname")
        display_name @tag(name: "dname")

        posts {
            title @filter(op: "=", value: ["%uname"])
                  @filter(op: "!=", value: ["%dname"])
                  @output
        }
    }
}

This finds posts where the title equals the author's username but differs from their display name.

docs.title: Scope and ordering
docs.text:
Tags must be defined before they are used in a @filter. The general rule is: - A tag must appear earlier in the query than any filter that uses it - Tags defined in parent scopes can be used in child scopes - Tags defined in sibling scopes cannot reference each other

# Valid: tag defined before use
{
    User {
        username @tag
        display_name @filter(op: "=", value: ["%username"])
    }
}

# Invalid: tag used before definition
{
    User {
        username @filter(op: "=", value: ["%display"])
        display_name @tag(name: "display")
    }
}

docs.title: @transform directive
docs.text: The @transform directive applies transformations to values. It's most commonly used with @fold to perform aggregations, but can also be used on individual values.

docs.title: Count operation
docs.text: Currently, the only supported operation is count, which counts the number of items in a list produced by @fold.

docs.title: Basic counting
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "post_count")
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "post_count": 3
}

docs.title: Counting with filters
docs.text:
You can filter before counting to count only items matching certain criteria:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @output(name: "popular_post_count")
        {
            likes @filter(op: ">", value: ["$min_likes"])
        }
    }
}

This counts only posts with more than $min_likes likes.

docs.title: Filtering on counts
docs.text:
Transform is commonly used with @filter to filter based on aggregated counts:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$threshold"])
              @output(name: "post_count")
    }
}

This only returns users who have at least $threshold posts.

docs.title: Count without output
docs.text:
You can use transform with filter without outputting the count:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">", value: ["$min_posts"])
        {
            # No outputs needed - we just need to verify the count
            __typename
        }
    }
}

This filters out users with $min_posts or fewer posts, without outputting the actual count.

docs.title: Multiple transforms in one query
docs.text:
You can use multiple transforms in different parts of a query:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @output(name: "post_count")

        follows @fold 
                @transform(op: "count")
                @output(name: "following_count")
    }
}

Result: 

{
    "username": "alice",
    "post_count": 5,
    "following_count": 12
}

docs.title: Transform with nested folds
docs.text:
When using nested folds, you can transform at each level:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @filter(op: ">", value: ["$min_posts"])
              @output(name: "post_count")
        {
            title @output

            comments @fold 
                     @transform(op: "count")
                     @output(name: "comment_count")
        }
    }
}

This returns users with more than $min_posts posts, and for each post, counts its comments.

docs.title: Using transform with filters inside folds
docs.text:
The transform operates on the filtered result:

{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold 
              @transform(op: "count")
              @output(name: "recent_post_count")
        {
            created_at @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$since_date"])
        }
    }
}

This counts only posts created on or after $since_date.

docs.title: Comparison operators with counts
docs.text:
All standard comparison operators work with counts:

# Equal to
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: "=", value: ["$exact_count"])

# Not equal to
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: "!=", value: ["$not_count"])

# Greater than
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: ">", value: ["$min_count"])

# Greater than or equal
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min_count"])

# Less than
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: "<", value: ["$max_count"])

# Less than or equal
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: "<=", value: ["$max_count"])

# One of (in a set)
posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: "one_of", value: ["$valid_counts"])

docs.title: Find items with no connections
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: "=", value: ["$zero"]) {
            __typename
        }
    }
}

With {"zero": 0}, this finds users with no posts.

docs.title: Find items with at least one connection
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @filter(op: ">", value: ["$zero"]) {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

This filters out users with no posts.

docs.title: Count range filtering
docs.text:
{
    User {
        username @output
        follows @fold 
                @transform(op: "count")
                @filter(op: ">=", value: ["$min"])
                @filter(op: "<=", value: ["$max"])
                @output(name: "following_count")
    }
}

This finds users following between $min and $max other users (inclusive).

docs.title: Transform requires fold
docs.text:
The @transform(op: "count") operation requires @fold to be present on the same edge:

# Invalid: transform without fold
{
    User {
        posts @transform(op: "count") {
            title @output
        }
    }
}

# Valid: transform with fold
{
    User {
        posts @fold @transform(op: "count") @output(name: "count")
    }
}

docs.title: Future operations
docs.text: Currently, only count is supported, but the @transform directive is designed to support additional operations in the future, such as sum, avg, min, and max.

docs.title: Type coercion
docs.text: Type coercion allows you to narrow down a vertex to a more specific type. This is similar to type casting or "instanceof" checks in programming languages and is particularly useful when working with interfaces and type hierarchies.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Type coercion is performed using GraphQL's inline fragment syntax with ... on TypeName:

{
    Number(max: 10) {
        value @output

        ... on Prime {
            # This scope only executes for Prime numbers
            is_prime: value @output
        }
    }
}

Results include is_prime only for prime numbers: 

{"value": 2, "is_prime": 2}
{"value": 3, "is_prime": 3}
{"value": 4}  // not prime, no is_prime field
{"value": 5, "is_prime": 5}

docs.title: Filtering by type
docs.text:
Type coercion acts as an implicit filter. Only vertices that are instances of the specified type continue in the coerced scope:

{
    Number(max: 20) {
        ... on Composite {
            # Only composite (non-prime) numbers
            value @output

            primeFactor @fold {
                factor: value @output
            }
        }
    }
}

This query only processes composite numbers and outputs their prime factors.

docs.title: Multiple type coercions
docs.text:
You can have multiple type coercions in the same query to handle different types separately:

{
    SearchResults(query: "example") {
        ... on User {
            type: __typename @output
            username @output
        }

        ... on Post {
            type: __typename @output
            title @output
        }

        ... on Comment {
            type: __typename @output
            text @output
        }
    }
}

Each search result is processed according to its actual type.

docs.title: Type coercion on edges
docs.text:
Type coercion can be applied after traversing an edge:

{
    Repository {
        name @output

        issue {
            ... on Bug {
                severity @output
                stack_trace @output
            }

            ... on FeatureRequest {
                priority @output
                estimated_effort @output
            }
        }
    }
}

This processes bugs and feature requests differently.

docs.title: Type coercion with interfaces
docs.text:
When a vertex implements an interface, you can coerce from the interface to specific implementing types:

{
    Webpage {  # Webpage is an interface
        url @output

        ... on User {
            # User-specific fields
            username @output
        }

        ... on Post {
            # Post-specific fields
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Nested type coercions
docs.text:
Type coercions can be nested:

{
    Number(max: 100) {
        ... on Composite {
            value @output

            primeFactor {
                ... on LargePrime {
                    # Only large prime factors
                    size_category @output
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Type coercion with filters
docs.text:
Combining type coercion with filters provides fine-grained control:

{
    Number(max: 50) {
        ... on Prime {
            value @filter(op: ">", value: ["$min"])
                  @output
        }
    }
}

This finds primes greater than $min.

docs.title: Type coercion with optional
docs.text:
Type coercion can be combined with @optional:

{
    User {
        username @output

        posts @optional {
            ... on FeaturedPost {
                featured_title: title @output
            }
        }
    }
}

If a user has no featured posts (either no posts at all, or no posts of the FeaturedPost type), featured_title is null.

docs.title: Type coercion with fold
docs.text:
Type coercion within a fold only aggregates vertices of the specified type:

{
    Repository {
        name @output

        issues @fold {
            ... on Bug {
                bug_title: title @output
            }
        }
    }
}

This creates a list of only bug titles, excluding other issue types.

docs.title: Type coercion with recurse
docs.text:
Type coercion can be used within recursive traversals:

{
    Number(max: 5) {
        value @output

        successor @recurse(depth: 10) {
            ... on Prime {
                prime: value @output
            }
        }
    }
}

This follows the successor chain but only outputs prime numbers encountered along the way.

docs.title: Accessing type information
docs.text:
The special field __typename returns the actual type of a vertex:

{
    Number(max: 10) {
        type: __typename @output
        value @output
    }
}

Result: 

{"type": "Zero", "value": 0}
{"type": "Prime", "value": 2}
{"type": "Prime", "value": 3}
{"type": "Composite", "value": 4}

docs.title: Valid coercions
docs.text: Type coercion is only valid when: 1. Coercing from an interface to a type that implements it 2. Coercing from a type to one of its subtypes (if the schema has inheritance)

docs.title: Invalid coercions
docs.text:
Type coercion is invalid when: 1. Coercing to an unrelated type 2. Coercing from a concrete type to a parent type (use the parent type directly instead) 3. Coercing to a non-existent type

# Invalid: User and Post are unrelated types
{
    User {
        ... on Post {  # Error!
            title @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Process different types differently
docs.text:
{
    SearchResults(query: "trustfall") {
        ... on Repository {
            repo_name: name @output
            stars @output
        }

        ... on User {
            username @output
            bio @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Filter to a specific subtype
docs.text:
{
    Shape {
        ... on Circle {
            # Only process circles
            radius @output
            area @output
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Conditional edges based on type
docs.text:
{
    Vehicle {
        model @output

        ... on ElectricVehicle {
            battery {
                capacity @output
            }
        }

        ... on GasVehicle {
            engine {
                displacement @output
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Trustfall schemas
docs.text:
Datasets in Trustfall are described using a schema. The schema describes the shape of each data point in the dataset, and how different data points are connected to each other.

The schema is used to validate and type-check queries, making sure they are valid before attempting to execute them. It also powers editor conveniences such as code auto-complete.

docs.title: Schema components overview
docs.text:
In Trustfall, all datasets are modelled as a graph, consisting of typed vertices containing properties, and connected to each other by edges.

Since editor auto-complete also relies on schema data, Trustfall directives are included in each Trustfall schema. Their definitions specify the query positions where each directive is valid and may be suggested as a code auto-completion. The schema directives section is always the same for any given Trustfall version, and must not be changed by hand.

docs.title: Example setup
docs.text:
Consider a hypothetical social media app called "Flutter" where users may post public messages, "like" each other's posts, and follow other users' activity.

In this section, we'll build up a Trustfall schema for the Flutter app step by step.

If you'd like to peek ahead, click here to reveal the final schema we'll build up to. 
schema {
    query: Entrypoints
}

type Entrypoints {
    """
    Find a specific user by their username, if they exist.
    """
    FindUser(username: String!): User

    """
    Run a search across all public posts with the given search terms.
    """
    SearchPosts(text: String!): [Post!]
}

"""
A piece of data that has its own webpage.
"""
interface Webpage {
    # properties
    """
    The human-readable URL at which this webpage may be visited.
    """
    url: String!
}

"""
A user account on Flutter.
"""
type User implements Webpage {
    # properties from Webpage
    """
    The URL of this user's profile page.
    """
    url: String!

    # own properties
    """
    The user's unique username. All users are required to have one.
    """
    username: String!

    """
    The name the user would like to be known by, if any was set.

    If the user has not set a display name, this value will be `null`.
    """
    display_name: String
    # end of properties

    # edges
    """
    The messages posted by this user, if any.
    """
    posts: [Post!]

    """
    The users this user follows, if any.
    """
    follows: [User!]
}

"""
A message posted by a Flutter user.
"""
type Post implements Webpage {
    # properties from Webpage
    """
    The URL of this post.
    """
    url: String!

    # own properties
    """
    The contents of the posted message.
    """
    message: String!

    # edges
    """
    The user who authored this post.

    Each post has precisely one author.
    """
    author: User!
}

docs.title: Vertex types and properties
docs.text:
A vertex is akin to a table in SQL. Consider our Flutter example, where we have users and their posts, and also other users they follow. If we were modelling it in SQL, we would have a User table and a Post table — therefore in Trustfall we have a User vertex and a Post vertex.

A vertex can have properties associated with it (similar to columns in SQL), and edges. We'll initially just focus on properties as these are the simplest case. For a user we can imagine the following properties as a minimum:

  • url: the URL to the users profile page (REQUIRED)
  • username: the unique username of the account (REQUIRED)
  • display_name: the name we display for the user (OPTIONAL)

With these two properties we can define a type for the schema called User which looks as follows:

"""
A user account on Flutter.
"""
type User {
    """
    The URL of this user's profile page.
    """
    url: String!

    """
    The user's unique username. All users are required to have one.
    """
    username: String!

    """
    The name the user would like to be known by, if any was set.

    If the user has not set a display name, this value will be `null`.
    """
    display_name: String
}

Here we've defined three string properties with doc comments to describe them. We've also made url and username required fields by adding the ! suffix to the type. This means that the value can't be null. Meanwhile, display_name is allowed to be null as it is just a String.

We'll now also define our Post type: it will be very similar, with a url to the post and a message representing the post. For now, the user who posted it will be omitted and covered in the next section.

"""
A message posted by a Flutter user.
"""
type Post implements Webpage {
    """
    The URL of this post.
    """
    url: String!

    """
    The contents of the posted message.
    """
    message: String!
}

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
We may also want to query data that refers to other vertices. This is what edges are for — relationships between other vertex types. For our user, these edges will be the posts the user has created, and a list of the other users they follow. We thus get the following schema for the User vertex type:

"""
A user account on Flutter.
"""
type User {
    # own properties
    """
    The URL of this user's profile page.
    """
    url: String!

    """
    The user's unique username. All users are required to have one.
    """
    username: String!

    """
    The name the user would like to be known by, if any was set.

    If the user has not set a display name, this value will be `null`.
    """
    display_name: String
    # end of properties

    # own edges
    """
    The messages posted by this user, if any.
    """
    posts: [Post!]

    """
    The users this user follows, if any.
    """
    follows: [User!]
}

For readability, here we've split properties and edges using non-doc comments such as # own edges.

As a user can make multiple posts and follow multiple people, the type of both edges is a list. Posts is a list of non-null post objects with the type [Post!] and follows is similar a list of non-null users [User!].

There are some nullability rules to be aware of with the Trustfall edges, these are all the valid forms of a Post edge:

  • Post is 0 or 1 post
  • Post! is exactly 1 post
  • [Post!] is 0 or more posts
  • [Post!]! is 1 or more posts

In our example the last one is the only one we won't be using. By making the list non-nullable [Post!]! it guarantees at least one value - whereas in normal GraphQL this can still be an empty list. We also can't specify the type as [Post] as having a list of multiple posts that can be null doesn't make sense — and would also complicate our queries.

Applying a similar change to Post we now add an edge for the author of the post, a single non-null User.

"""
A message posted by a Flutter user.
"""
type Post {
    # own properties
    """
    The URL of this post.
    """
    url: String!

    """
    The contents of the posted message.
    """
    message: String!

    # edges
    """
    The user who authored this post.

    Each post has precisely one author.
    """
    author: User!
}

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
Both the User and Post vertex types have a url field, we can therefore have them both implement the same interface. Interfaces are similar to GraphQL and programming languages which use them in that we can define a set of properties an interface must provide and also set our edge and query types to be interfaces instead of concrete types. Let's add a webpage interface to contain the URL field and have our vertex types implement it:

"""
A piece of data that has its own webpage.
"""
interface Webpage {
    # properties
    """
    The human-readable URL at which this webpage may be visited.
    """
    url: String!
}

"""
A user account on Flutter.
"""
type User implements Webpage {
    # properties from Webpage
    """
    The URL of this user's profile page.
    """
    url: String!

    # own properties
    """
    The user's unique username. All users are required to have one.
    """
    username: String!

    """
    The name the user would like to be known by, if any was set.

    If the user has not set a display name, this value will be `null`.
    """
    display_name: String
    # end of properties

    # own edges
    """
    The messages posted by this user, if any.
    """
    posts: [Post!]

    """
    The users this user follows, if any.
    """
    follows: [User!]
}

"""
A message posted by a Flutter user.
"""
type Post implements Webpage {
    # properties from Webpage
    """
    The URL of this post.
    """
    url: String!

    # own properties
    """
    The contents of the posted message.
    """
    message: String!

    # own edges
    """
    The user who authored this post.

    Each post has precisely one author.
    """
    author: User!
}

docs.title: Entrypoints
docs.text:
An entrypoint gives us an initial set of vertices to work with. Each Trustfall schema needs a root element called schema with a field query that is our entrypoint type — the starting point of the query.

In the entrypoint we want to provide the means to query our data source for the initial set of vertices we'll consider and filter or transform. For data sources like APIs we'll usually define some entrypoints that map to API endpoints. If all of our data is available without restrictions, like in a SQL database, we might just define simple entrypoints named after (and returning a list of) each vertex type. Although, even in that case we may want to add some more sophisticated entrypoints, to simplify some operations that might be complicated or impossible to express in a Trustfall query.

For this hypothetical Flutter app, we'll define an entrypoint type with two queries:

  1. Find a user by their username
  2. Search for posts with a given search query

Adding this into the schema would look like the following:

schema {
    query: Entrypoints
}

type Entrypoints {
    """
    Find a specific user by their username, if they exist.
    """
    FindUser(username: String!): User

    """
    Run a search across all public posts with the given search terms.
    """
    SearchPosts(text: String!): [Post!]
}

Here our FindUser query takes a non-null string argument username and returns a User which may or may not be null. The SearchPosts query takes a non-null string argument text and returns a list of non-null Post where the list would be empty if there were no matching posts.

docs.title: Overview of the Trustfall query engine
docs.text:
Trustfall's goal is to turn every piece of data into a database that can be explored, queried, and combined with other databases.

Querying shouldn't be reserved just for SQL and NoSQL databases! Trustfall offers a query language that can be used over any kind of data source, such as REST APIs, JSON files, source code repositories.

For example: the cargo-semver-checks linter uses Trustfall queries to catch and prevent breaking changes that violate semantic versioning (SemVer) in the Rust programming language. Its queries operate over a data model derived from JSON and TOML data. An example of such a query is "find functions that have been removed from the package's public API."

docs.title: Comparing Trustfall to GraphQL
docs.text:
Trustfall aims to be more expressive and more performant than GraphQL. It supports functionality like recursive and left joins, aggregations, arbitrary filter clauses, and lazy evaluation —— none of which are in GraphQL. It also performs well with high query complexities: real-world Trustfall use cases can often have deeply nested or widely-branching queries covering 20 edges (joins) or more.

GraphQL is superior when aiming to drive a UI, especially one written in React. GraphQL's nested, eagerly-evaluated output is preferable here: UI queries are usually small and simple, without too much branching nor many levels of nesting.

docs.title: Comparing Trustfall to SQL
docs.text:
Trustfall aims to be better suited for querying data that isn't already available in SQL database format, such as data in REST APIs, JSON files, source code repositories, or AI tools. Its lazy evaluation model and flexible optimization API excel when getting query data is expensive in performance or monetary cost, such as when using pay-per-request or rate-limited APIs. These same properties also make Trustfall excellent at joining multiple data sources together.

If all required data is already in a SQL database, SQL will offer superior performance and should be preferred over Trustfall.
